usage: time adverbial; 과거에는 sets up an explicit contrast with 지금/현재
collocation with 돌아보다 (reflect); also 과거를 회상하다
pairs with 먼/가까운 to mark how far back the time is
ask about / dredge up someone's past
과거를 묻지 마세요 = don't ask about my past
examples: 과거에는 여기가 다 논밭이었어요.
In the past, this whole place was rice fields.
과거에(는) frames a then-vs-now contrast
이제 과거는 잊고 앞으로 나아가려고 해요.
Now I'll forget the past and move forward.
과거 as 'bygones' you leave behind, paired with 앞으로
그 사람의 과거에 대해서는 저도 잘 몰라요.
Even I don't really know about that person's past.
과거 = someone's personal history; -에 대해서 = about
nuance: 과거 is Sino-Korean (過去, 過 'pass' + 去 'go away', literally 'what has gone by'), the past as an abstract span that sits in a tidy set with 현재 (present) and 미래 (future); it also means a person's personal history and, in grammar, the past tense (과거형). The key dividing line is with 예전 and 옛날: those are the warm, conversational words for 'a while back / the old days,' whereas 과거 is cooler, more analytical and at home in writing, news and reflection (과거를 돌아보다). The pitfall for English speakers is reaching for 과거 to translate 'last time' or 'a while ago' in casual chat — that slot belongs to 저번/예전, and 과거 there sounds oddly philosophical. Also remember 과거 is a noun, never a verb: 'in the past it was…' is 과거에는 ~였어요, not 과거했어요.

과거 is a noun, not a verb; 'in the past it was a school' is 과거에는 학교였어요, never 과거했어요 (no such verb).
Dropping the topic particle in a contrast (과거에 vs 과거에는) loses the 'used to, but now…' nuance; add 는 when you mean to contrast with the present.

usage: stands alone as a sentence-initial adverb with no particle
현재까지의 결과 = the results so far
set phrase in news, reports and announcements
as of now / based on the present
현재 기준으로 = taking this moment as the reference point
examples: 현재 서울에 살고 있어요.
I'm currently living in Seoul.
현재 used adverbially, with NO 에 attached
현재까지 신청한 사람이 백 명이 넘어요.
So far, over a hundred people have applied.
현재까지 = counting up to this moment
과거나 미래보다 현재가 가장 중요해요.
The present matters more than the past or future.
현재 as a noun contrasted with 과거 and 미래
nuance: 현재 is Sino-Korean (現在, 現 'appear/manifest' + 在 'exist', literally 'what now exists'), serving both as the noun 'the present' and as an adverb 'currently / at present.' Its nearest rival is 지금, and the line between them is register, not meaning: 지금 is the everyday spoken word, while 현재 is its formal, written twin that fills reports, news tickers and official notices (현재 상황, 현재까지). The classic English-speaker pitfall is treating 현재 like an English noun and bolting 에 onto it: you say 현재 살고 있어요, never 현재에 살고 있어요 — as an adverb it stands bare. A second trap is overusing 현재 in friendly conversation, where it can sound stiff and bureaucratic; switch to 지금 the moment the tone relaxes.

Don't confuse 현재 (present) with 현실 (現實, reality); 현실 is 'real life / actuality', a different concept even though both start with 현.

usage: broad time adverbial for things yet to come
pairs with 밝은/어두운 to color one's outlook
examples: 미래에는 자동차가 하늘을 날지도 몰라요.
In the future, cars might fly through the sky.
미래에(는) for broad predictions; -지도 몰라요 = might
아이들의 밝은 미래를 위해 열심히 일해요.
I work hard for the children's bright future.
밝은 미래 collocation; -를 위해 = for the sake of
먼 미래보다 가까운 미래를 먼저 계획하세요.
Plan for the near future before the distant one.
가까운/먼 미래 contrast
nuance: 미래 is Sino-Korean (未來, 未 'not yet' + 來 'come', literally 'what has not yet come'), the future as a broad abstract concept that completes the trio with 과거 and 현재; it loves adjectives like 밝은/어두운 and verbs like 준비하다 and 계획하다. The sharp contrast to learn is 미래 vs 앞으로/나중에: 미래 is the panoramic, somewhat formal 'the future' you'd put in an essay or a speech, while 앞으로 ('from now on') and 나중에 ('later') handle concrete, near-term plans in real conversation. So the English-speaker pitfall is saying 미래에 ~할 거예요 for a personal intention like 'in the future I'll exercise more' — a Korean naturally says 앞으로 ~할 거예요; 미래에 there sounds grandiose. Likewise 'later today / soon' is 나중에/이따가, never 미래.

usage: points back to a specific instant just mentioned
보는 순간 = the instant one sees; always present 는
adverb for a split-second, reflexive reaction
pairs with 결정적인/마지막 for a crucial instant
examples: 그 순간 머릿속이 하얘졌어요.
At that moment my mind went blank.
그 순간 = at that very instant
문을 여는 순간 깜짝 놀랐어요.
The instant I opened the door, I was startled.
-는 순간 stays present even for a past event
행복한 순간들은 늘 빨리 지나가는 것 같아요.
Happy moments always seem to pass by quickly.
순간 as a countable noun + 들; pairs with 지나가다
nuance: 순간 is Sino-Korean (瞬間, 瞬 'blink of an eye' + 間 'interval', literally 'the space of a blink'), so it is a razor-thin instant — far shorter than 동안 (a stretch you endure) or 시기 (a phase). Its most powerful use is the pattern Verb-는 순간 ('the very moment that…'), the go-to for dramatic timing, and 순간적으로 for a reflexive, in-a-flash action. The synonym to keep apart is 잠깐/잠시: those mean 'for a little while' (a short duration), whereas 순간 is a single point with no duration — so 'please wait a moment' is 잠깐만요, never 순간만요. The other classic English-speaker trap is conjugating that pattern into the past: even for a past event you keep the present 는, as in 문을 여는 순간 놀랐어요, not 연 순간.

usage: a particular stretch of time defined by what's happening
시기 follows a noun naming the phase
pairs with 적절한/적당한 for an opportune moment
놓치다 = to let the opportune timing slip by
examples: 지금이 이사하기에 가장 좋은 시기예요.
Now is the best time to move.
시기 = an opportune phase for doing something
취업을 준비하는 시기에는 스트레스가 많아요.
During the job-hunting period, there's a lot of stress.
-는 시기에(는) = during the phase of
좋은 시기를 놓치지 않으려고 서둘렀어요.
I hurried so as not to miss the good timing.
시기를 놓치다 collocation; -지 않으려고 = so as not to
nuance: 시기 is Sino-Korean (時期, 時 'time' + 期 'term/period'), a phase of time defined by what is happening within it — broader than a 순간 but narrower than 시대 (an era like 조선 시대). It carries a strong flavor of 'the right timing' for an action, hence 적절한 시기 and 시기를 놓치다. The crucial contrast is 시기 vs 기간 (期間, a measured duration with a clear start and end): 시험 기간 ('the 3-day exam period' you can count) versus 성장 시기 ('the growing phase,' a qualitative stage) — English 'period' covers both, which is exactly why learners mix them up. A pure homophone hazard: 시기 also exists as a separate word meaning 'envy/jealousy' (猜忌), so context, not sound, tells them apart. Use 기간 when you can put a number of days on it; use 시기 for a named phase or the opportune moment.

usage: at that time, in those days
the most common form; a past time already in context
사고 당시 = at the time of the accident
set phrase in accounts, reports and testimony
examples: 그 당시에는 휴대폰이 없어서 정말 불편했어요.
Back then there were no cell phones, so it was really inconvenient.
그 당시에(는) = in those days, contrasting with now
사고 당시 저는 집에 있었어요.
At the time of the accident, I was at home.
N 당시 attaches straight to the event noun
당시 저는 아직 대학생이었어요.
At that time, I was still a university student.
당시 placed before the clause it frames
nuance: 당시 is Sino-Korean (當時, 當 'the very / corresponding' + 時 'time', literally 'that very time'), and it always points back to a specific past time already fixed in context, so it lives in forms like 그 당시 and N 당시 (사고 당시, 졸업 당시). The sharp contrast to master is 당시 vs 그때: both mean 'at that time,' but 그때 is the neutral, everyday spoken word, while 당시 is its formal cousin that belongs in narration, news reports and written testimony — say 그때 to a friend, 당시 in an essay. The English-speaker pitfalls are two: first, 당시 is anchored to the past only, so you can never use it for 'now' or the future; second, learners try to use it bare as a free-standing adverb, but it normally rides on 그 or an event noun (그 당시에는, 사고 당시), not floating alone like English 'at the time.'

In casual conversation 그때 sounds far more natural than 당시; 당시 can feel like written news copy among friends.
Don't use 당시 bare to mean 'at the time' out of nowhere; it needs an anchor — 그 당시 or an event noun like 사고 당시.

usage: the core adverbial; almost always carries 에
two actions together, or a dual quality
거의 softens to 'nearly at the same instant'
examples: 두 사람이 동시에 같은 말을 했어요.
The two of them said the same thing at the same time.
동시에 = simultaneously
그는 가수인 동시에 배우예요.
He is a singer and at the same time an actor.
N인 동시에 = is X and also Y
문이 닫히는 동시에 비가 쏟아지기 시작했어요.
The instant the door closed, rain started pouring down.
-는 동시에 = simultaneously with the action
nuance: 동시 is Sino-Korean (同時, 同 'same' + 時 'time', literally 'same time') and almost never stands alone — it lives as 동시에 ('simultaneously') or in the patterns -는 동시에 (with a verb: two actions at once) and N인 동시에 (with a noun: 'is X and also Y', two qualities at once, as in 가수인 동시에 배우). The contrast to nail is 동시에 vs 한꺼번에: 동시에 means precisely 'at the same instant' (two events lined up in time), while 한꺼번에 means 'all in one go / in a single batch' (quantity bundled together), so 'I paid it all at once' is 한꺼번에 냈어요, not 동시에 냈어요. The main English-speaker pitfalls: (1) using bare 동시 where you need 동시에 — the 에 is almost obligatory; and (2) reaching for 동시에 when you really mean 'all together in one batch,' which is 한꺼번에.

usage: compound: a workplace one keeps for life
never forget for one's whole life
examples: 할머니는 평생 이 마을에서 사셨어요.
Grandmother lived in this village her whole life.
평생 used adverbially = 'all her life'; -셨- honorific
이 은혜는 평생 잊지 않을게요.
I'll never forget this kindness as long as I live.
평생 + negative = 'never in my life'
평생 한 번 있을까 말까 한 기회예요.
It's a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.
평생 한 번 stressing rarity across a whole life
nuance: 평생 is Sino-Korean (平生, 平 'level/ordinary' + 生 'life', literally 'the ordinary course of a life', i.e. one's entire lifespan) and is used mostly as an adverb ('for my whole life') with no particle, or as 평생 동안. It carries real emotional weight, which is why it powers heartfelt promises (평생 사랑할게요) and statements of rarity (평생 한 번). The synonym to contrast is 일생 (一生): 일생 is the bookish, biographical 'a lifetime' you meet in a written life-story, while 평생 is the warm, spoken word that feels personal and felt rather than clinical. The English-speaker pitfall is over-stacking the meaning: 평생 already contains 'whole,' so 평생 전체 is redundant — just say 평생 or 평생 동안. Also note 평생 typically modifies a verb directly (평생 살다, 평생 기억하다), so don't force an extra particle onto it as if it were an object.

usage: 순서대로 하다 = do things in the proper order
keep the order, wait one's turn
다음 순서는 누구예요? = whose turn is next?
examples: 번호 순서대로 들어가시면 됩니다.
You may go in in numerical order.
순서대로 = following the sequence; -면 됩니다 = it's fine to
줄을 서서 순서를 지켜 주세요.
Please line up and wait your turn.
순서를 지키다 = observe the proper order
발표 순서가 갑자기 바뀌었어요.
The presentation order suddenly changed.
순서가 바뀌다 collocation
nuance: 순서 is Sino-Korean (順序, 順 'follow/comply' + 序 'sequence/order', literally 'the sequence one follows'), meaning the order or arrangement in which things are lined up or done, and by extension a person's 'turn.' Two set phrases are essential: 순서대로 ('in order') and 순서를 지키다 ('keep the order / wait your turn'). The synonym to contrast is 차례 (次例/次序): 차례 leans toward an individual's turn in a rotation ('it's my turn now' is most idiomatically 이제 제 차례예요), while 순서 emphasizes the overall sequence or arrangement of the whole set. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'do it in order' is 순서대로 하다, with the special 대로 ('according to'); 순서로 하다 sounds incomplete and learners habitually drop the 대로. Also note 순서 (sequence) is distinct from 차이 (difference) and 차례 (turn) even though all feel related in English.

For 'it's my turn now,' 이제 제 차례예요 is more idiomatic than 제 순서예요; 차례 highlights the turn, 순서 the whole sequence.
순서 is a noun; 'put them in order' uses a verb like 순서대로 놓다/정리하다, not a non-existent 순서하다.

usage: 이 축제의 시초 = the origin of this festival
X이/가 시초가 되다 = X marks the beginning
거슬러 올라가다 = go back upstream to the source
examples: 이 작은 가게가 그 회사의 시초였어요.
This small shop was the beginning of that company.
N의 시초였다 = was the origin of N
사소한 말다툼이 큰 싸움의 시초가 됐어요.
A trivial argument became the start of a big fight.
시초가 되다 = to mark the beginning of
그 발견이 현대 의학의 시초라고 해요.
That discovery is said to be the start of modern medicine.
시초 for a historical starting point; -라고 해요 = it's said
nuance: 시초 is Sino-Korean (始初, both 始 and 初 mean 'beginning' — a doubled 'begin-begin' that stresses the very first origin point), the source from which something all started. It is decidedly formal and 'origin/historical' in flavor, unlike the everyday 처음 ('first time / at first') or 시작 ('the start of an activity'). The contrast to fix: 시작 is the act of starting and is used constantly in speech (수업을 시작하다 = start class), whereas 시초 names the originating point of something larger — a company, a custom, a conflict — and appears as N의 시초 or 시초가 되다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 시초 for casual 'at first / in the beginning' — that is 처음(에), not 시초. And because 시초 is a noun naming an origin, there is no verb 시초하다; to start an action you must use 시작하다.

Don't confuse 시초 (origin) with 시작 (the start/launch of an activity); you launch a class with 시작, you trace a custom's roots with 시초.

english: the final stage, the home stretch
usage: 막바지에 이르다 = to reach the final stage
접어들다 = to move into a stage/phase
summer is in its final days
N이/가 막바지다 = N is winding down
examples: 공사가 이제 막바지에 접어들었어요.
The construction has now entered its final stage.
막바지에 접어들다 = enter the home stretch
시험 준비가 막바지라서 정말 바빠요.
Exam prep is in its final stretch, so I'm really busy.
N이/가 막바지다 = is in its last phase; -라서 = so/because
올해도 어느덧 막바지에 이르렀네요.
This year too has reached its final days before we knew it.
막바지에 이르다 collocation; 어느덧 = before one realizes
nuance: 막바지 is native Korean (from 막 'the very last / the end' + 바지, a phase-marking element), meaning the very last stretch of something that has been underway for a while — a season, a project, a year — exactly 'the home stretch' or 'final phase,' usually with a feel of intensity or winding down just before the end. The contrast to master is 막바지 vs 마지막: 마지막 simply means 'the last (one/item)' of a set (마지막 페이지 = the last page), with no sense of process, whereas 막바지 is the final ongoing phase of something that takes time. A close colloquial cousin is 막판 (a more casual 'the last round / final stretch'). The English-speaker pitfalls: don't use 막바지 for 'the last one/item' (that is 마지막), and pair it with the right verbs — 막바지에 이르다/접어들다/다다르다 ('reach/enter the home stretch'), not 막바지에 가다.

막바지 implies something has been going on for a while; don't apply it to a brand-new task that just started — there's no 'final phase' yet.

english: in the meantime, during that time
usage: often with 에; marks the interval between two points
change a lot in the meantime
did something happen in the meantime?
asking about events during the gap
can't endure even that short interval
그사이를 못 참고 = unable to wait even that briefly
examples: 잠깐 나갔다 왔는데 그사이에 비가 왔나 봐요.
I just stepped out and back, and it seems it rained in the meantime.
그사이에 = during that short interval; -나 봐요 = it seems
오랜만에 만났는데 그사이 아이가 많이 컸네요.
It's been a while since I saw them, and the child has grown so much in the meantime.
그사이 stressing change over the gap
제가 자리를 비운 그사이에 무슨 일 있었어요?
Did something happen while I was away?
그사이에 = in the gap when one was absent
nuance: 그사이 (그 'that' + 사이 'gap/interval'; also written spaced as 그 사이) means 'in the meantime / during that interval' — the gap between two moments, typically while someone was away or time quietly slipped past, and it very often appears as 그사이에 alongside a remark about unexpected change. The contrast to lock in is 그사이 vs 그동안: 그동안 covers a longer, continuous stretch ('all this while, over the whole period' — 그동안 잘 지냈어요?), whereas 그사이 zooms in on a shorter in-between gap, often surprisingly eventful for its brevity. The main English-speaker pitfalls: (1) reaching for 그동안 when you mean a brief 'while I was gone' gap (use 그사이) or vice versa; and (2) spelling worry — both 그사이 (one word) and 그 사이 (spaced) are accepted, so just stay consistent within your text rather than agonizing over it.

그사이 marks an interval between two points, so it needs that two-point framing; using it for an open-ended 'these days' (요즘) is wrong.
Both 그사이 and 그 사이 are accepted spellings; pick one and stay consistent rather than mixing them in the same piece of writing.

english: (the old) days, one's time/era of life
usage: the most common collocation, full of nostalgia
refers fondly to a remembered period
pairs with 좋은/힘든 to color the remembered period
examples: 학창 시절이 가끔 너무 그리워요.
I sometimes miss my school days so much.
학창 시절 = one's school years; 그립다 = to miss/long for
어린 시절에는 시골에서 자랐어요.
In my childhood, I grew up in the countryside.
어린 시절에(는) = during one's young days
그 시절에는 다들 가난했지만 행복했어요.
In those days everyone was poor but happy.
그 시절 evoking a nostalgic era; -지만 = but
nuance: 시절 is Sino-Korean (時節, 時 'time' + 節 'season/segment', literally a 'season of time'), and it names a remembered stage of one's life almost always tinged with nostalgia — 학창 시절 (school days), 어린 시절 (childhood), 그 시절 (those days). The contrast to feel is 시절 vs 시기 and 때: 시기 is a neutral, analytical phase (성장 시기 = the growth period) and 때 is a plain 'time when…,' whereas 시절 is warm, personal and backward-looking, glowing with fondness. The English-speaker pitfalls: (1) 시절 looks back — you cannot use it for a future or coolly neutral period, so 'a difficult time ahead' is not 어려운 시절 in the future sense; and (2) 시절 almost always rides on a descriptor (학창/어린/그/좋은), so using it bare to mean just 'time' sounds unfinished — you need that modifier to evoke the remembered stage.
